raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening, pregnancy-associated myocardial disease characterized by acute-onset heart failure and severe left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, typically defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) under 45%. This clinical entity manifests in late pregnancy or during the early postpartum months in women without pre-existing heart disease [1]. The global epidemiology of PPCM is highly heterogeneous, with marked variations in incidence. While it affects approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births in the United States, far higher incidences are documented in regions like South Africa (1 in 1,000) and Haiti (1 in 300) [2,3]. Established risk factors include maternal age over 30 years, multiparity, multiple gestations, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (such as preeclampsia), black race, and prolonged use of tocolytics [4,5]. Despite advancements in intensive obstetric care, PPCM remains one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and peripartum cardiovascular mortality globally [6].

The pathophysiology of PPCM was long considered elusive, but recent molecular breakthroughs have clarified its multi-hit etiology. A key mechanism is the oxidative stress-protease-prolactin axis [7]. During late pregnancy and postpartum, increased oxidative stress in the myocardium triggers the upregulation of cathepsin D, a lysosomal enzyme that cleaves the full-length 23 kDa prolactin hormone into a toxic 16 kDa fragment [8]. This 16 kDa prolactin isoform is strongly angiostatic, pro-apoptotic, and pro-inflammatory, damaging the coronary microvasculature and causing cardiomyocyte dysfunction [9]. Furthermore, an angiogenic imbalance occurs, driven by high circulating levels of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), an anti-angiogenic protein secreted by the placenta that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [10,11]. Additionally, genetic studies have identified a shared genetic architecture between PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Approximately 15% to 20% of PPCM patients harbor pathogenic gene mutations, most commonly truncating variants in the titin gene (*TTN*), highlighting a genetic predisposition that is unmasked by the physiological stress of pregnancy [12,13,14].

Clinical presentation ranges from mild congestive symptoms to fulminant cardiogenic shock, ventricular arrhythmias, and thromboembolic events [15]. Because common symptoms of PPCM—such as dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema—overlap with physiological changes of late pregnancy and the normal postpartum period, delay in diagnosis is frequent and dangerous [16,17]. Diagnostic workup relies heavily on transthoracic echocardiography to confirm an LVEF < 45% and exclude other cardiac etiologies [18]. Serum biomarkers are highly valuable; elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels assist in differentiating PPCM from normal physiological states, while cardiac troponins indicate ongoing myocardial injury [19,20].

Therapeutic management of PPCM focuses on standard heart failure regimens, carefully tailored to gestational status to ensure fetal safety [21]. Prior to delivery, conventional heart failure drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) are strictly contraindicated due to their teratogenicity and risk of fetal renal dysgenesis [22]. Instead, afterload reduction is achieved using a combination of hydralazine and organic nitrates [23]. Beta-blockers, specifically beta-1 selective agents like metoprolol succinate, should be initiated in stable patients [24]. Post-delivery, standard guideline-directed medical therapy can be fully optimized, including the introduction of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) and ARNIs [25].

Based on the pathophysiological role of the 16 kDa prolactin fragment, the addition of bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary, has emerged as a disease-specific treatment [26]. Multicenter clinical trials have demonstrated that bromocriptine, when added to standard heart failure therapy (the "BOARD" regimen), significantly improves LV recovery rates and clinical outcomes compared to standard therapy alone [27]. Due to the prothrombotic state of the postpartum period and the potential of bromocriptine to increase thromboembolic risk, prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation (using heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) must be co-administered during bromocriptine treatment [28].

The prognosis of PPCM is generally more favorable than that of other non-ischemic cardiomyopathies, with a substantial proportion of patients achieving full recovery of LV function within six months [29]. However, those with persistent LV dysfunction face a high risk of adverse events. Crucially, subsequent pregnancies in women with a history of PPCM carry a high risk of recurrence and further clinical deterioration, even among those who have fully recovered their LVEF, necessitating detailed pre-conception counseling and multidisciplinary care [30].
